chapters.title: Chapter 3: Models That Are Actually Used in Practice

lessons.title: Tree-Based Models: Random Forest and Gradient Boosting for Trading Signals

children.text: Lesson 9 closed on a gap: a linear model cannot capture the idea that momentum might predict returns more reliably in calm markets than in turbulent ones, unless you manually build that interaction as its own feature. Tree-based models close this gap by design, they split data on one feature at a time, in sequence, so a split on momentum can end up living entirely inside a branch already defined by a volatility split. Nobody has to tell the model that interaction exists in advance.

body.text: A decision tree naturally captures interactions and non-linear relationships by repeatedly splitting data on feature thresholds. A single tree overfits badly on noisy data, it can memorize every training example, including its noise. The fix, used by both random forests and gradient boosting, is never to trust one tree, but to combine the predictions of many imperfect ones.

children.text: A Single Decision Tree: Powerful and Dangerously Overfit

A decision tree repeatedly asks a simple question: is this feature above or below some threshold, then splits the data accordingly and repeats inside each resulting branch. Grown deep enough, a tree can carve out a branch for almost every individual training example, effectively memorizing the training set, noise included, which is the same overfitting problem Chapter 1 warned about, taken to an extreme. This is not a reason to avoid trees. It is the reason nobody trades with a single one.
Random Forest: Averaging Away the Overfitting

markDefs.definition: An ensemble method that trains many decision trees, each on a random bootstrap sample of the training rows and a random subset of features at each split, then averages or votes across all of them to make a final prediction.

children.text: builds many independent trees in parallel, each trained on a random bootstrap sample of the training rows and a random subset of features considered at each split, then averages their predictions, or has them vote, for a final answer. Because each individual tree overfits differently, in its own random way, averaging across hundreds of them cancels out much of that noise, while genuine patterns that most trees independently arrive at tend to survive. The result is a model that is meaningfully harder to badly overfit than any single tree, and a strong, reliable default baseline for tree-based trading signals.
Gradient Boosting: Trees That Learn From Each Other's Mistakes

Gradient boosting takes a different approach: trees are built one at a time, in sequence, and each new tree is trained specifically to correct the errors the trees before it are still making, rather than being trained independently. Implemented through libraries like XGBoost and LightGBM, the industry standard on quant desks handling Indian and global equity data alike, gradient boosting generally reaches a higher ceiling than a random forest. That extra power comes with extra responsibility: an unconstrained boosted model, too many trees, no shrinkage on how much each new tree can correct, no early stopping against a genuinely held-out validation window, will overfit more aggressively than a random forest given the same noisy data.

cells: Many independent trees, trained in parallel on bootstrapped samples, then averaged
Robust, hard to badly overfit, a solid default baseline
Ceiling can be lower than a well-tuned boosted model
Trees trained sequentially, each correcting the previous trees' errors
Often the highest ceiling of the two, widely used via XGBoost and LightGBM
Prone to overfitting without careful regularization and genuine walk-forward validation

body.text: A more flexible model does not just risk overfitting more, it is also better at exploiting any leftover leak in your pipeline. A linear model might get a small, noticeable accuracy bump from a leaked feature. A deep, unconstrained gradient boosting model can turn that same small leak into near-perfect training accuracy, hiding the mistake even more convincingly, precisely because it is powerful enough to fit almost anything, leaked signal included. Every leakage check from Chapters 1 and 2 matters more, not less, once you move to tree-based models.

children.text: Feature Importance: A Basic Sanity Check, Not the Full Picture

Tree-based models offer a built-in feature importance score, roughly, how much each feature contributed to reducing error across all the splits that used it. This is a useful first-pass sanity check: if a feature you built for a clear economic reason, momentum, or distance from a moving average, barely registers, that is worth investigating, and if a feature you cannot explain dominates the model, that is worth investigating even more, it may be a subtle leak from Chapter 1 or 2 rather than a genuine pattern. Basic feature importance has real limits though, particularly with correlated features like momentum measured over several overlapping windows, where credit can get split arbitrarily between them. A more rigorous approach, such as SHAP values, gives a fuller picture and is covered properly in this course's advanced sequel.

body.caption: Fitting a random forest and a gradient boosting model, and checking feature importance
body.code:
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier, GradientBoostingClassifier

# Tree-based models do not need the Lesson 6 feature scaling step,
# they split on raw thresholds, not distances, so scale is irrelevant to them
rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, max_depth=5, random_state=42)
rf.fit(X_train, y_train)

gb = GradientBoostingClassifier(n_estimators=200, max_depth=3, learning_rate=0.05, random_state=42)
gb.fit(X_train, y_train)

# A basic sanity check: does the model actually lean on features that make economic sense?
for name, importance in sorted(zip(feature_names, rf.feature_importances_), key=lambda x: -x[1]):
    print(f"{name}: {importance:.3f}")

body.title: Why the leak matters more here
body.question: A researcher's feature set has an accidental leak, a rolling window computed with center=True, the exact mistake from Lesson 3. She fits both a Ridge regression and an unconstrained, deep gradient boosting model on the same leaky data. What should she expect?
options: Both models will be affected by the leak identically, since the underlying data is the same
The gradient boosting model is likely to exploit the leak far more aggressively, producing an even more misleadingly high training accuracy than the Ridge model
Tree-based models are immune to data leakage because they do not use scaled features
Neither model will be affected, since data leakage only impacts linear models
body.explanation: A more flexible model is better at fitting whatever signal is available, including leaked, illegitimate signal. An unconstrained gradient boosting model can bend itself around a leak far more completely than a linear model's limited functional form allows, which is exactly why this lesson stresses that leakage checks matter more, not less, as model flexibility increases.

body.title: Choosing between random forest and gradient boosting
body.scenario: A systematizing trader is building his first tree-based model on Nifty 50 stock data. He has limited time to carefully tune hyperparameters and validate against multiple walk-forward windows, and would rather have something reasonably reliable now than risk a badly overfit model from a technique he has not fully mastered yet.
body.prompt: Given this trader's constraints, would a random forest or a gradient boosting model be the more sensible starting point, and why?
body.modelAnswer: A random forest is the more sensible starting point here. Its independent, parallel trees and averaging make it meaningfully harder to badly overfit even with fairly default settings, which suits a trader who does not yet have the time or experience to carefully regularize and validate a more powerful but more overfitting-prone gradient boosting model. Gradient boosting likely offers a higher ceiling eventually, but realizing that ceiling safely requires exactly the careful tuning and walk-forward validation discipline this trader says he does not yet have time for, which makes it the better second step, not the first one.

cards.definition: A model that repeatedly splits data based on feature thresholds, naturally capturing non-linear relationships and interactions between features.
An ensemble method that trains many decision trees, each on a random bootstrap sample of rows and a random subset of features, then averages or votes across all of them.
An ensemble method that trains trees sequentially, with each new tree specifically correcting the errors of the trees trained before it.
A random sample of the training rows, drawn with replacement, used to train each individual tree in a random forest.
A score, produced by tree-based models, describing roughly how much each feature contributed to reducing error across all the splits that used it.

points: Tree-based models naturally capture interactions and non-linear relationships that a plain linear model can only represent if you manually engineer them.
A single decision tree overfits severely on noisy data. Random forest and gradient boosting both fix this by combining many trees rather than trusting one.
Random forest trains many independent trees in parallel and averages them, making it a robust, hard-to-badly-overfit default baseline.

Gradient boosting trains trees sequentially, each correcting the last, often reaching a higher ceiling but requiring more careful regularization and genuine walk-forward validation to avoid overfitting.

More flexible models exploit data leaks more aggressively than simpler ones, which means the leakage discipline from Chapters 1 and 2 becomes more important, not less, once tree-based models enter the picture.
Basic feature importance is a useful sanity check, confirming a model leans on economically sensible features, but a fuller picture, such as SHAP values, is covered in this course's advanced sequel.
